source_text: Quis nollet curam nos agere animae de uictu et corpori de uestitu, nisi qui ista homini ante prospexit et exinde praestans merito curam eorum tamquam aemulam liberalitatis suae prohibet,
thought_title: Why the Provider forbids our anxiety
pass_a_gloss: Who would be unwilling for us to take care for the soul about food and for the body about clothing, except the one who foresaw these things for man beforehand, and from then on, supplying them, rightly forbids care about them as if it were a rival to his own generosity,
pass_b_english: Who would not want us to care for the soul about food and for the body about clothing, except the one who foresaw these things for man beforehand, and who therefore, as the one supplying them, rightly forbids our anxiety over them as a rival to his own generosity (Luke 12:22–23)?

choices.why: Luke 12:22 context: μὴ μεριμνᾶτε; Tertullian's cura here is anxious care

choices.english: as though it were competing with his generosity
rejected: as an insult to his bounty

bible_refs.note: anima/esca, corpus/uestimentum; Tertullian is expounding Luke 12:22-28

notes: Sentence continues in the source (ravens, lilies, Solomon); this saying ends at prohibet, so the excerpt closes the clause there.
Repair per checker a: homini kept; soul/food and body/clothing pairing kept; exinde praestans and prohibet inside the nisi qui clause.
